axes.model_access: The platform ships no model itself; AI nodes reach external LLMs via per-vendor credentials (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google etc. through the LangChain node family and dedicated nodes); the node coverage list has not been verified item by item — the official nodes docs are authoritative. When self-hosted, model credentials live on your own instance.
axes.runtime: Two official forms: self-hosted (Docker/npm, free Community edition with no execution cap) and n8n Cloud managed subscription. Self-hosted queue mode (worker scaling) is included in Community; multi-main HA belongs to paid tiers (official choose-n8n framing, 2026-10 third-party paraphrase cross-checked against official docs).
axes.local_files: A self-hosted instance runs on your own machine/server — workflow data, credentials and execution logs all land in your own environment; external storage for binary data (S3 etc.) is a paid tier. In the Cloud form, data sits in n8n's cloud.
axes.background: Workflows are executed by the instance: a continuously running self-hosted instance carries scheduled and webhook triggers; the official docs provide Cron/queue mechanisms. "Keeps running when your laptop is off" depends on where you run the instance — the platform does not hold executions for you after shutdown.
axes.tools: The core is the integration-node ecosystem (officially "hundreds of integrations", not verified item by item); MCP is named explicitly in the official license FAQ ("configuring workflows through the n8n editor, your UI, the n8n API, MCP or an AI agent" is one of the commercial-license scenarios) — MCP is an officially supported usage surface.
axes.context: In-workflow data transformation and sub-workflow passing are the main axis; cross-workflow persistent memory mechanisms have not been verified item by item (unknown means unknown). Credentials and execution data persist per instance.
axes.permissions: Self-hosted permission boundary = your instance boundary; in Community, workflows/credentials are accessible only to their creator and the instance owner (sharing is a paid tier). Enterprise SSO/RBAC unlocks via Business/Enterprise license keys. The license boundary matters more than the permission boundary: SUL's three restrictions see the license field.
axes.fit: Fits: cross-system automation as the main axis, embedding AI nodes into existing flows, self-hosting to control data. Does not fit: wrapping n8n into your product to sell to customers (needs a commercial agreement); pure-code orchestration (go to framework); out-of-the-box multi-tenant SaaS (Community has no sharing).

sections.许可是它最该先读的一页:
The official Community license page states SUL's three restrictions (key points paraphrased): use only for **your own internal business or non-commercial personal purposes**; redistribution must be **free of charge and non-commercial**; the license and copyright notices may not be removed. Files whose names contain `.ee.` fall under the Enterprise License.

The official help center adds case-law-style guidance: running workflows for a client on your own instance while the client only receives the results — allowed; the client entering the editor or configuring workflows through your UI/API/MCP/AI agent — requires a commercial agreement (n8n Embed).
